title: Show HN: Topothesy – a daily online geography game
description: I'm not very good at geography and don't know the exact locations of many cities. That's why it is hard for me to play games where you have to pin cities precisely on a map. But what if you place cities relative to other cities? That's how idea of a puzzle was born: given a set of cities, choose any five and place them correctly relative to other on a 5x5 grid. The topmost city is the northernmost, the leftmost is the westernmost. There should be only one city in each row and column, since the cities are not strictly vertical or horizontal relative to each other. The goal of the game is to try to find the most compact set of cities. If cities are far from each other, it is quite easy to place them; on the other hand such set will be far from compact. It is much harder to find a compact set and to place it correctly. The main challenge in developing the game was to make it moderately difficult. It is quite easy to place Los Angeles and Sydney, but much harder to place Osaka and Kyoto. Another issue is to make it interesting every day: it is not interesting to place Zurich, Milan and Marseille too often. So, I want to ask: 1. Are the rules clear? Have you encountered some difficulties? 2. Is the game interesting? Is it too hard or too easy? 3. I feel that it can be used for learning, but I don't know how. Any ideas? Thank you very much in advance. The puzzle is available here: https://www.topothesy.com Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50558556 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

I wanted something where every device in the network can act as a self node, and it'll be a Mesh of devices interconnected. title: Show HN: Open-source customer-facing agents
description: Hi, Dmitri from Radioso here, an open-source platform to design AI agents for customers and visitors in any channel, in the style of Fin/Ada/Decagon. The repo is https://github.com/radioso-ai/radioso and our website is https://radioso.ai Today, your choices are: 1. Buy a very expensive service for your vertical (usually starting with $$ five figures monthly) 2. Get a cheap off-the-shelf chatbot that mostly answers FAQs 3. Build your own, and then also build the inbox, human handoff, audit trail and integrations around it At Radioso we wanted an open-source option that combines the best of all 3. You can integrate it with your own software via API/SDK or your CRM, or run it standalone, either self-hosted or in our cloud. The engine runs multi-step interactions and takes actions: calling your APIs, updating records, booking things. Maybe you’ve tried Parlant; Radioso is the alternative “with batteries included”: RAG, audit trail, customer service inbox, and integrations like Slack and email. Under the hood it’s plain TypeScript + PostgreSQL, works with OpenAI/Anthropic/other models, and is licensed under Apache 2.0 which includes all features (The only thing we keep under EE license is the multi-tenant layer we use to run our own cloud). We have existing customers running it for technical Q&A, course booking, online product recommendations and goods returns, among others, some reaching 92% of conversations automated. We’re currently working on voice support so we can offer a call center. Our ambition is to be “the WordPress of customer-facing AI” :), where people can contribute their favorite plugins and benefit from the ecosystem. Longer term, we think browsing the web will mostly mean talking to your own agent, and when you need a service or a purchase, your agent will talk to the vendor’s agent to get things done. For this, Radioso already publishes an A2A Agent Card and we’re working on the rest. Your Radioso services are also callable over MCP, for customers who already use it. Thanks for your attention. We’d especially love to hear which integrations you’d want, whether you’d self-host it, and what’s stopped you from deploying a customer-facing AI agent so far. Tell us what you think. title: Show HN: Sheetgraph, AI agents can understand complex spreadsheets
description: Hi guys, I built a tool www.lovespreadsheets.com earlier this year and a huge problem we kept running into is processing messy, real-world, complex spreadsheets for AI agents. Even a "medium" sized spreadsheet converts to about 1m+ tokens if read fully, which immediately blows up the current context windows of most models. So I noticed most agents sample data from spreadsheets in chunks instead. So I (& Claude) built this library Sheetgraph, https://github.com/asharma327/sheetgraph , to compress spreadsheets (~100x compression) while still maintaining their structure (like a dependency graph for formulas) & other relevant metadata such as macros, cell data types, formatting. There is a zipped full workbook of the spreadsheet as well for the agent to lookup data as needed. Still rough around the edges so would love any feedback on both the idea and any details. This is used in our primary product + services platform Love Spreadsheets so we are actively maintaining and improving it. Thanks! title: Show HN: We mapped data center regulations across 50 states and 1,462 localities
description: Hi HN! My company Regbase tracks regulatory developments around the world for compliance teams at major corporations. Ahead of the midterm elections we decided to do an in-depth survey of all state and local regulations around data centers. We built an interactive map showing the data center policies across the United States. It covers all 50 states and 1,462 localities across legislation, regulations and executive orders. We collected and analyzed the data using our platform. Every result has a link to the official source so you can read the policy for yourself. Here's some interesting things we learned: - Moratoriums (temporary bans) are the most common instrument. We counted 1,010 in total with an average duration of 10 months. - Starting around October 2025, most policies switched from tax incentives to bans and restrictions. This correlates with increased energy prices and worsening public sentiment towards AI. - When construction is allowed, it's very common for protections to be put in place particularly around electricity and less for water. Many of the bans are actually refusals to issue these licenses. We would love your feedback! In particular please let us know if there is any other data that would be useful or interesting to see. title: Show HN: Pretty Git Tree – Your Git history as generative art
description: I've spent months building something complex and (so far) invisible. I know that the number of commits, branches, merges etc. aren't proof of progress, but what I needed was a way to represent the amount of effort I'd put in that wasn't "proximity to burnout". Pretty-git-tree takes in your git history (just the commit structure, and it stays local to your browser) and gives you a visually interesting representation of it. For my own projects I use the "qubits" style which winds a quantum circuit around a space-filling curve. I've included snapshots of some famous git repositories as well. I didn't want to just use the standard git tree, because I felt that there were so many different ways of exploring the data - plus I wanted it to look good at the top of a weekly standup report. I've included the four styles I expect people to use, plus another 15 or so styles in the repo where I wanted to try things out (like rendering the branches as tower-blocks in a city, or kintsugi fractures).
